idea: Harrison's H4 marine chronometer engraving (public-domain plate) with the caption 'Longitude: a problem solved by a clockmaker the experts ignored.' Black ink on white; for people who love an outsider proven right.

Waldseemüller 1507 map, the first to name 'America', cropped to the lettering of the word AMERICA on the sliver of South America, with the caption 'Named by a man who never went.' A smart joke about who gets credit.
A 16th-century Olaus Magnus sea monster from the Carta Marina, mid-attack on a ship, captioned 'Margin of error.' Mapmakers' honesty about uncertainty, as a joke.

Blank white interior of an old Africa map, as in Jonathan Swift's verse, with only the engraved elephants kept and the caption 'Where geographers lacked knowledge, they drew elephants.' Becomes a statement about faking certainty.

Mercator's 1569 projection with Greenland and Africa shown at true relative size via a drawn-in-code overlay of Africa's outline sitting over Greenland, caption 'Not to scale. Neither is your problem.' For map nerds who want a point of view.

A historic compass rose engraving where every point is relabelled by hand-lettered type: 'Lost', 'Probably lost', 'Not lost, exploring', 'Definitely lost', and so on around the dial. Warm, funny, wearable.
John Snow's 1854 Broad Street cholera map (public domain) with the single pump circled and the caption 'Data, not a miasma.' Honors the map that changed epidemiology.
Piri Reis 1513 map fragment with a gazelle-skin coastline and the caption 'Drawn from twenty charts and one confession.' Reflects how he credited sources in the map itself.
Antique terrestrial globe gore strips (the flat printed segments) laid out like a peeled orange, captioned 'Every map is a flattened lie, beautifully.' Lovely object, sharp attitude.

Matthew Fontaine Maury's wind and current chart engraving cropped to its swirling arrows, captioned 'The sea has roads. Someone had to read them.' Nerdy admiration for data gathered from old logbooks.
A Ptolemy-style world map engraving (1482 Ulm edition) with the Indian Ocean as a closed lake and the caption 'Confidently wrong for 1,400 years.' For people who love an authority overthrown.

An 1890s Admiralty chart of an uncharted bay with a single sounding number written in huge type, '?', in the middle of otherwise blank water, caption 'Depth: unknown. Proceed.' A quiet motto for risk-takers.
The Tabula Peutingeriana Roman road map stretched into a long ribbon wrapping the shirt, with a tiny added caption, 'Roads all lead somewhere. Check the scale.' Rewards close looking.
Hereford Mappa Mundi's tiny engraved figures (Sciapods, one-footed men) with the caption 'First reviews of the unexplored.' Wry nod to medieval travel hearsay.

Cook's Endeavour track chart of New Zealand (1770, public domain) with the coastline outlined and the caption 'Off by about 40 miles at Banks Peninsula. Island.' Funny trivia about the famous mapped-as-island error.
An engraved sextant and octant plate (18th-century instruments catalogue) with the caption 'Find yourself with a bright star and some arithmetic.' Lovely object, hopeful message.
A Polynesian stick chart (Marshall Islands, public-domain museum photo traced as line art) captioned 'A map of waves, not of land.' Honors wayfinding that charts swells instead of coastlines.
The 1569 Ortelius atlas sea monster 'Iceland' plate with the monster wearing a tiny drawn-in-code hat of a mapmaker's cartouche, caption 'Atlas of things we hadn't seen yet.' Playful and well made.

Shackleton's Endurance expedition map line of the James Caird boat route, with a thin drawn-in-code dotted path ending in the text 'Eight hundred miles in a lifeboat. The group chat was shorter.' Awe plus dry humor.

A Ptolemaic map's blank southern edge captioned 'Terra Incognita' in the original engraver's lettering, with a drawn pencil addition below: 'Now accepting reservations.' Reframes the unknown as invitation.
